albumInfo.summary: What's Going On is the eleventh studio album by the American soul singer Marvin Gaye. It was released on May 21, 1971, by the Motown Records subsidiary label Tamla. Recorded between 1970 and 1971 in sessions at Hitsville U.S.A., Golden World, United Sound Studios in Detroit, and at The Sound Factory in West Hollywood, California, it was Gaye's first album to credit him as producer and to credit Motown's in-house session musicians, known as the Funk Brothers.

listeningNotes: Listen for the incredible layered vocal arrangements - Marvin often sang multiple parts himself, creating a choir-like effect.
Notice how the songs flow seamlessly into each other, creating a continuous suite rather than separate tracks.
Pay attention to the jazzy, sophisticated instrumentation that blends traditional Motown with more complex orchestral arrangements.

trackGuide.guide: The opening track sets the tone with its gentle, questioning melody and socially conscious lyrics. Listen for the distinctive flute intro and Marvin's layered vocal harmonies.
trackGuide.focus: Social conscience and musical innovation

trackGuide.guide: Marvin Gaye wrote this deeply personal tribute to his brother Frankie, who served three years in Vietnam. Listen for the mournful flute doubling the vocal melody, the understated congas, and how the arrangement leaves space around Marvin's voice — the sparseness mirrors the emotional weight of a soldier's return.
trackGuide.focus: Personal narrative and Vietnam War impact

trackGuide.guide: Gaye's meditation on heroin addiction uses deceptively gentle bossa nova rhythms and lush strings to mask its darkness. The contrast between the soaring orchestral arrangement and lyrics about 'the friendly sky' — a euphemism for the high — creates one of soul music's most unsettling juxtapositions.
trackGuide.focus: Addiction and contrast

trackGuide.guide: A brief but powerful interlude built around a repeating four-note ascending motif. Gaye's layered backing vocals create a gospel choir effect, while the lyrical plea for future generations anchors the album's moral vision — this is the hinge point between the album's social critique and its spiritual redemption arc.
trackGuide.focus: Hope and future generations

trackGuide.guide: At under two minutes, this is the album's shortest track but its most intricate vocal arrangement. Gaye triple-tracked his voice into a self-harmonizing gospel quartet, with the Funky Brothers providing a slow, church-like groove underneath. The lyric reflects Gaye's renewed faith after years of personal turmoil.
trackGuide.focus: Spirituality and vocal arrangement

trackGuide.guide: Perhaps the album's most famous track, featuring a haunting melody and lyrics that were remarkably prescient about environmental concerns.
trackGuide.focus: Environmental awareness

trackGuide.guide: The album's climax features extended improvisation and some of Marvin's most passionate vocal performances.
trackGuide.focus: Climax and musical freedom

trackGuide.guide: The penultimate track brings the album's spiritual thread to a climax. Gaye recorded multiple vocal takes and layered them into a virtual choir, while the arrangement swells from a whisper to a full orchestral crescendo. The song's message of universal unity prefigures the conscious soul movement of the early 1970s.
trackGuide.focus: Spirituality and closure

trackGuide.trackTitle: Inner City Blues (Make Me Wanna Holler)
trackGuide.guide: The powerful closing track that paints a vivid picture of urban poverty and economic inequality, ending the album on a note of unresolved tension.
trackGuide.focus: Urban poverty and social commentary

source.label: Wikipedia
source.title: Pet Sounds
source.extract: Pet Sounds is the eleventh studio album by the American rock band the Beach Boys, released on May 16, 1966, by Capitol Records. It was produced, arranged, and primarily composed by Brian Wilson with guest lyricist Tony Asher. Recorded largely between January and April 1966, it furthered the orchestral sound introduced in The Beach Boys Today! (1965). Seeking to expand Phil Spector's Wall of Sound technique and surpass the Beatles' Rubber Soul (1965), Wilson's orchestrations blended pop, jazz, exotica, classical, and avant-garde elements, combining rock instrumentation with layered vocal harmonies, found sounds, and instruments not normally associated with rock. It was their first album in which studio musicians, such as the Wrecking Crew, largely replaced the band on their instruments, and the first in which any rock group abandoned the small-ensemble format for an entire album. Its unprecedented total production cost exceeded $70,000.

listeningNotes: Listen for the unconventional instruments: electro-theremin on 'Shordown', bicycle bells on 'You Still Believe in Me', and Coca-Cola cans used as percussion.
Notice the unprecedented vocal harmonies - Brian often recorded himself singing multiple parts to create rich, complex choral effects.
Pay attention to the innovative production techniques like tape splicing and varispeed that create the album's distinctive sound.

trackGuide.guide: Brian Wilson collaborated with Tony Asher on this deceptively complex opener — listen for the startling key change on the word 'nice,' the syncopated drum fills by Hal Blaine, and the twelve-string guitar shimmer that creates the track's sun-drenched euphoria while masking lyrics of pure teenage frustration.
trackGuide.focus: Musical sophistication and innovation

trackGuide.guide: Track 2 of 13, "You Still Believe In Me", is the album's early-album track and runs 2:36. In the album sequence it follows "Wouldn't It Be Nice" and leads into "That's Not Me". No confident track-specific external source was found, so this entry uses static track metadata only.

trackGuide.guide: Mike Love's lead vocal anchors this introspective track, but the real innovation is in the arrangement: the distinctive tack piano (thumbtacks in the hammers for a percussive twang), the gradual build of backing vocals, and the use of silence between phrases that creates a confessional, almost awkward intimacy.
trackGuide.focus: Lyrical maturity

trackGuide.trackTitle: Don't Talk (Put Your Head On My Shoulder)
trackGuide.guide: Features one of the album's most complex vocal arrangements and demonstrates Brian's growing influence from classical music and jazz harmonies.
trackGuide.focus: Complex vocal arrangements

trackGuide.guide: Uses a prominent electro-theremin, an early electronic instrument that gives the track its distinctive, otherworldly quality.
trackGuide.focus: Electro-theremin and electronic innovation

trackGuide.guide: An entirely instrumental track that showcases Brian's arranging skills with its intricate orchestration and absence of vocals.
trackGuide.focus: Instrumental arrangement and orchestration

trackGuide.guide: A reworked traditional folk song that demonstrates Brian's ability to transform existing material through sophisticated arranging and production.
trackGuide.focus: Arrangement and transformation

trackGuide.guide: Often cited as one of the greatest love songs ever written, features innovative secular use of religious language and complex harmonic structure.
trackGuide.focus: Lyrical innovation and harmonic complexity

trackGuide.guide: Features lyrics that reflect Brian's interest in Eastern philosophy and psychedelic exploration, with innovative instrumental breaks.
trackGuide.focus: Philosophical themes and instrumental innovation

trackGuide.guide: Shows Brian's growing ability to write poignant, melancholic pop songs with sophisticated melodic construction.
trackGuide.focus: Melodic sophistication and melancholy

trackGuide.trackTitle: I Just Wasn't Made for These Times
trackGuide.guide: The album's emotional core finds Brian Wilson singing his most autobiographical lyrics through a theremin's ethereal wail. Hal Blaine's tympani rolls punctuate each verse like thunder, while the complex key changes — shifting mood with each modulation — mirror the instability Wilson describes in the lyric.
trackGuide.focus: Autobiographical content and alienation

trackGuide.guide: The title track features innovative use of space and silence in its arrangement, creating a distinctive atmospheric quality.
trackGuide.focus: Atmospheric arrangement and use of space

trackGuide.guide: The album's closing track features one of the most famous fading endings in recording history and lyrics that poignantly address lost love and innocence.
trackGuide.focus: Innovative ending and lyrical poignancy

artistInfo.summary: Roberta Joan "Joni" Mitchell is a Canadian singer-songwriter, multi-instrumentalist, and painter. As one of the most influential singer-songwriters to emerge from the 1960s folk music circuit, Mitchell became known for her personal lyrics and unconventional compositions, which grew to incorporate elements of pop, jazz, rock, and other genres. Among her accolades are eleven Grammy Awards, and induction into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1997.

albumInfo.summary: Blue is the fourth studio album by the Canadian singer-songwriter Joni Mitchell, released on June 22, 1971, by Reprise Records. Written and produced by Mitchell, it was recorded in 1971 at A&M Studios in Hollywood, California. Created just after her breakup with Graham Nash and during an intense relationship with James Taylor, Blue explores various facets of relationships from love on "A Case of You" to insecurity on "This Flight Tonight".

source.label: Wikipedia
source.title: Blue (Joni Mitchell album)
source.extract: Blue is the fourth studio album by the Canadian singer-songwriter Joni Mitchell, released on June 22, 1971, by Reprise Records. Written and produced by Mitchell, it was recorded in 1971 at A&M Studios in Hollywood, California. Created just after her breakup with Graham Nash and during an intense relationship with James Taylor, Blue explores various facets of relationships from love on "A Case of You" to insecurity on "This Flight Tonight". The songs feature simple accompaniments on piano, guitar and Appalachian dulcimer. The album peaked at number 3 on the UK Albums Chart, number 9 on the Canadian RPM Albums Chart and number 15 on the Billboard 200.

listeningNotes: Listen for Mitchell's distinctive use of alternative guitar tunings, which create unique chord voicings and resonant qualities not possible in standard tuning.
Notice the incredible intimacy of her vocal performances - many tracks were recorded in single takes with minimal instrumentation.
Pay attention to the lyrical specificity and poetic imagery that makes each song feel both deeply personal and universally relatable.

trackGuide.guide: The album closer features Mitchell's distinctive open-tuned guitar work creating a drone-like bed for her vocal. The lyric cycles back to the album's opening themes of searching and restlessness, creating a circular structure that mirrors the journey's incompleteness — the seeking never resolves, it only deepens.
trackGuide.focus: Intimate tone and lyrical themes

trackGuide.guide: Features a distinctive bass line and tells the story of Mitchell's relationship with Chuck Mitchell, showcasing her ability to blend personal narrative with musical sophistication.
trackGuide.focus: Personal narrative and musical sophistication

trackGuide.guide: One of the album's most emotionally raw tracks, written about a daughter Mitchell gave up for adoption, featuring particularly poignant lyrics and melody.
trackGuide.focus: Emotional rawness and personal history

trackGuide.guide: The title track features Mitchell's distinctive voice at its most vulnerable, with simple guitar accompaniment that allows the lyrics and melody to shine.
trackGuide.focus: Vocal vulnerability and simplicity

trackGuide.guide: Shows Mitchell's ability to create vivid, picturesque lyrics that paint a nostalgic view of her home state while hinting at underlying melancholy.
trackGuide.focus: Vivid imagery and nostalgia

trackGuide.guide: Mitchell's account of leaving a lover (believed to be James Taylor) is propelled by her urgent fingerpicking and a sudden electric guitar burst that simulates a plane's turbulence. The lyric's stream-of-consciousness quality — stars, engines, departure lounges — captures the dislocation of mid-flight heartbreak.
trackGuide.focus: Emotional intensity and relationship themes

trackGuide.guide: One of the album's most famous tracks, featuring Mitchell's distinctive piano playing and lyrics that blend Christmas imagery with personal heartbreak.
trackGuide.focus: Piano performance and seasonal imagery

trackGuide.guide: Often cited as one of Mitchell's greatest love songs, features the famous line 'I could drink a case of you, darling, and I would still be on my feet' and showcases her ability to blend metaphor with emotional directness.
trackGuide.focus: Metaphorical language and emotional directness

trackGuide.trackTitle: The Last Time I Saw Richard
trackGuide.guide: Mitchell recounts a barroom conversation with The Band's Richard Manuel, tracing his descent from idealistic youth to bitter cynicism. The piano-driven arrangement is unusually dark for Mitchell — the descending chord progression mirrors Richard's fall, while her vocal shifts from observational detachment to raw empathy.
trackGuide.focus: Poetic lyrics and melodic sophistication

listeningNotes: On 'Love's In Need of Love Today', listen for how the multitracked vocal harmonies gradually layer in, with Wonder's lead floating above a quiet Rhodes piano before the full band enters after two minutes.

The instrumental 'Contusion' showcases Wonder's drumming and a tight jazz-funk arrangement; the electric piano and synthesizer trade rapid-fire lines with a distorted guitar that darts in and out of the mix.

In 'Pastime Paradise', the synthetic string section is actually a Yamaha GX-1, and the juxtaposition of a gospel choir with lyrics about urban decay creates an eerie tension that's heightened by the absence of a bass drum until the final minute.

During 'As', the chord progression cycles through a series of key changes that never fully resolve, while the backing vocals—sung by Wonder, Mary Lee Whitney, and others—build into a call-and-response climax over the song's seven-minute run.

sources.title: Stevie Wonder
sources.extract: Stevland Hardaway Morris, known professionally as Stevie Wonder, is an American singer-songwriter, musician, and record producer. He is widely regarded as one of the most influential musicians of the 20th century, and is credited as a pioneer and influence by musicians across a range of genres that include R&B, pop, soul, gospel, funk, and jazz. A virtual one-man band during much of his peak years, Wonder's use of synthesizers and other electronic musical instruments in the 1970s reshaped the conventions of contemporary R&B. He also helped drive such genres into the album era, crafting his LPs as cohesive and consistent, in addition to socially conscious statements with complex compositions.

sources.extract: "Knocks Me Off My Feet" is a song written and performed by American recording artist Stevie Wonder, from his 1976 album Songs in the Key of Life. It was not released as a single, though it was released as a B-side to "I Ain't Gonna Stand for It" four years later, in 1980. albumInfo.summary: Abbey Road is the eleventh studio album by the English rock band the Beatles, released on 26 September 1969, by Apple Records. It is the last album the group recorded, although Let It Be (1970) was the last album completed before the band's break-up in April 1970. Abbey Road was mostly recorded in April, July, and August 1969, and topped the record charts in both the United States and the United Kingdom.

listeningNotes: In 'Come Together', focus on Paul McCartney's bass line, which slides and syncopates around Lennon's swampy vocal, while the electric piano was processed through a Leslie speaker to give it a watery, swirling texture.

The nine-part vocal harmony on 'Because' was triple-tracked by Lennon, McCartney, and Harrison, each singing their part three times to create an otherworldly chorale; the chord sequence is Beethoven's 'Moonlight Sonata' played in reverse.

During the medley, listen for the seamless transition from 'Sun King' to 'Mean Mr. Mustard': the final organ chord of 'Sun King' fades as Ringo's hi-hat count-in for 'Mustard' emerges, a trick achieved by punching in the tape at the exact moment.

On 'The End', Ringo Starr recorded his only drum solo in the Beatles' catalog, using eight microphones to capture his kit; immediately after, Paul, George, and John trade two-bar guitar solos in rotation, each with a distinct tone—McCartney's jagged, Harrison's melodic, Lennon's feedback-laden.

trackGuide.guide: Lennon's swamp-rock opener was built on a Chuck Berry-inspired riff, but slowed to a menacing crawl. The lyrics are a collage of absurdist imagery, and the song's tension comes from the contrast between the tight rhythm section and Lennon's detached, echo-heavy vocal.

sources.title: Maxwell's Silver Hammer
sources.extract: "Maxwell's Silver Hammer" is a song by the English rock band the Beatles from their 1969 album Abbey Road. Written by Paul McCartney and credited to the Lennon–McCartney partnership, it tells the tale of Maxwell Edison, a student who murders people with a hammer. The dark lyrics are disguised by an upbeat sound. McCartney described the song as symbolic of the downfalls of life, being "my analogy for when something goes wrong out of the blue, as it so often does."

sources.title: Oh! Darling
sources.extract: "Oh! Darling" is a song by the English rock band the Beatles, appearing as the fourth song on their eleventh studio album Abbey Road (1969). It was written primarily by Paul McCartney and credited to Lennon–McCartney. Its working title was "Oh! Darling ". Although not issued as a single in either the United Kingdom or the United States, a regional subsidiary of Capitol successfully edited it as a single in Central America, having "Maxwell's Silver Hammer" as its B-side. It was also issued as a single in Portugal. Apple Records released "Oh! Darling" in Japan with "Here Comes the Sun" in June 1970.

sources.title: Octopus's Garden
sources.extract: "Octopus's Garden" is a song by the English rock band the Beatles, written and sung by Ringo Starr, from their 1969 album Abbey Road. George Harrison, who assisted Starr with the song, commented: "'Octopus's Garden' is Ringo's song. It's only the second song Ringo wrote, and it's lovely." He added that the song gets very deep into the listener's consciousness "because it's so peaceful. I suppose Ringo is writing cosmic songs these days without even realising it." It was the last song released by the Beatles featuring Starr on lead vocals.

sources.extract: "I Want You (She's So Heavy)" is a song by the English rock band the Beatles, written by John Lennon and credited to Lennon–McCartney. The song closes side one of their 1969 album Abbey Road and features Billy Preston on Hammond organ. It was the first song recorded for Abbey Road but one of the last on the album to be finished; the band gathered in the studio to mix the song on 20 August 1969, marking the final time that all four Beatles were together in the studio.

sources.title: Here Comes the Sun
sources.extract: "Here Comes the Sun" is a song by the English rock band the Beatles from their eleventh studio album Abbey Road (1969). It was written and sung by George Harrison, and is one of his best-known compositions. Harrison wrote the song in early 1969 at the country house of his friend Eric Clapton, where Harrison had chosen to play truant for the day to avoid attending a meeting at the Beatles' Apple Corps organisation. The lyrics reflect his relief at the arrival of spring and the temporary respite he was experiencing from the band's business affairs.

trackGuide.guide: Cobain's four-chord opening riff — the 'Teen Spirit' riff — borrowed its quiet-loud-quiet dynamic from the Pixies' 'Gigantic.' Producer Butch Vig recorded over 70 vocal takes for the chorus alone, while Dave Grohl's thunderous drum entrance at 0:36 announces the arrival of grunge to the mainstream. The song's structure (verse-chorus-verse-solo-chorus) is deliberately simple — the power is in the delivery.

Written about the jocks who'd eventually become Nirvana fans without understanding the band's irony, set to a pop melody built for arenas. Grohl's disco-influenced hi-hat pattern and the Beach Boys-inspired backing vocals epitomize Cobain's pop instincts hidden in punk clothing — the joke was on everyone who made it a hit.

listeningNotes: On 'Dreams', the drum pattern is deceptively simple: Mick Fleetwood plays a single kick on beat one and a snare on beat three, with dampened toms that create a soft thud, leaving space for Nicks's husky vocal and the Rhodes electric piano.

The acoustic guitar on 'Never Going Back Again' is a fingerpicked DADGAD-tuned pattern played by Buckingham, double-tracked to create a shimmering stereo effect; there are no other instruments, just two voices intertwined.

In 'The Chain', listen for the moment at 2:45 when the song drops into a driving bass-and-drum breakdown—John McVie's bass line was originally improvised as a warm-up exercise and was later spliced into the final arrangement, becoming the section used as the BBC's Formula One theme.

During 'Gold Dust Woman', the final minute dissolves into a wash of backward cymbals, a howling electric guitar processed through a Leslie speaker, and Nicks's voice cracking as she wails, a raw moment captured in a single take at 4 a.m. after a long night of recording.

sources.title: Go Your Own Way
sources.extract: "Go Your Own Way" is a song by the British-American rock band Fleetwood Mac from their eleventh studio album, Rumours (1977). The song was released as the album's lead single on 20 December 1976 in the United States. Written and sung by Lindsey Buckingham, it became the band's first top-ten hit in the United States. "Go Your Own Way" has been well received by music critics and was ranked number 120 by Rolling Stone magazine on their list of 500 greatest songs of all time in 2010, and re-ranked number 401 in 2021. They also ranked the song second on their list of the 50 greatest Fleetwood Mac songs.

source.extract: Purple Rain is the sixth studio album by American musician Prince, featuring his backing band the Revolution. It was released on June 25, 1984, by Warner Bros. Records as the soundtrack album to the 1984 film of the same name. Purple Rain was musically denser than Prince's previous albums, emphasizing full band performances, and multiple layers of guitars, keyboards, electronic synthesizer effects, drum machines, and other instruments. Much of the album has a grandiose, synthesized, and psychedelic substance to the production and performances.

listeningNotes: On 'When Doves Cry,' note the total absence of bass guitar and bass synth—the track’s low end comes only from the kick drum and Prince’s baritone vocal layers, a decision made during a rough mix that Prince insisted on keeping.

The title track’s guitar solo was captured live at a 1983 benefit concert; listen for the moment at 5:12 when the band drops out and Prince’s sustained bent note hangs over the crowd noise before the final chorus.
In 'The Beautiful Ones,' focus on the three-octave vocal climb starting around 2:30—Prince moves from whispered croon to full-throated scream, with no instrumental build to cushion the leap.

The LinnDrum LM-1 patterns across the album are heavily customized—on 'Computer Blue,' the hi-hat programming shifts from sixteenth-note rigidity to loose triplet feels that mirror the song’s fractured structure.

trackGuide.guide: The album opens with Prince's mock-sermon — 'Dearly beloved, we are gathered here today to get through this thing called life' — before exploding into a synth-driven rock rave. The Oberheim OB-Xa riff and call-and-response guitar duel between Prince and Wendy Melvoin in the outro established him as both a pop star and a guitar virtuoso.

trackGuide.guide: Opens with a reversed cymbal swell before a grinding rock riff and a lyric so sexually explicit it triggered Senate hearings. The production layers a distorted drum machine under live cymbals, and Prince’s vocal shifts from snarling verse to a helium-pitched chorus in the span of a bar.

trackGuide.guide: Prince eliminated the bass guitar entirely from the mix — an unprecedented choice for a dance-pop single — leaving only a Linn LM-1 drum machine, synthesizer stabs, and his multi-tracked voice. The resulting claustrophobic sound perfectly mirrors the lyric's depiction of parental conflict and inherited dysfunction, and the song held the #1 spot for five weeks.

trackGuide.guide: A relentless synth-pop pulse built around a single chord progression that never resolves, creating a sense of forward motion without arrival. Prince's lyric deliberately blurs messianic imagery with romantic devotion — 'I'm not a woman, I'm not a man' — while the minimal arrangement keeps the focus squarely on his most direct vocal performance.

trackGuide.guide: Recorded live at First Avenue in Minneapolis on August 3, 1983, this was Prince's first performance with guitarist Wendy Melvoin. The 8:41 track features one of rock's most cathartic solos — Prince heard Bob Seger's live album and wanted to capture that energy. Clare Fischer's string arrangement adds cinematic grandeur to the raw live foundation.

sources.title: Let's Go Crazy
sources.extract: "Let's Go Crazy" is a 1984 song by Prince and The Revolution, from the album Purple Rain. It is the opening track on both the album and the film Purple Rain. "Let's Go Crazy" was one of Prince's most popular songs, and was a staple for concert performances, often segueing into other hits. When released as a single, the song became Prince's second number-one hit on the Billboard Hot 100, and also topped the two component charts, the Hot R&B/Hip-Hop Songs and Hot Dance Club Play charts, as well as becoming a UK Top 10 hit. The B-side was the lyrically controversial "Erotic City". In the UK, the song was released as a double A-side with "Take Me with U".

sources.title: Computer Blue
sources.extract: "Computer Blue" is a song by Prince and The Revolution. Released on June 25, 1984, it is the fourth track on Prince's sixth album, Purple Rain, which also served as the soundtrack to the film of the same name. In the film, the song represents Prince's character's angst at the budding relationship between the characters played by Morris Day and Apollonia, the latter of whom he desires, and he performs it in front of the two during The Revolution's set at a nightclub with the aim of upsetting them. The song was composed by Prince with credit to his father, John L. Nelson, for the guitar solo based on a piano instrumental written by Nelson and Prince. He titled the instrumental piece "Father's Song" and recorded it on piano for the film, though onscreen it was portrayed as being played by Prince's character's father, played by Clarence Williams III. On the box-set Purple Rain Deluxe (2017), a different and longer recording of "Father's Song" was included.

sources.title: Darling Nikki
sources.extract: "Darling Nikki" is a song produced, arranged, composed, and performed by American musician Prince, originally released on his sixth studio album Purple Rain (1984). Though the song was not released as a single, it gained wide notoriety after Tipper Gore pointed out its sexual lyrics—in particular an explicit reference to female masturbation—and was partly responsible for the creation of the Parental Advisory sticker. The song tells the story of a "sex fiend" named Nikki who seduces the singer.

sources.title: When Doves Cry
sources.extract: "When Doves Cry" is a song by American musician Prince, and the lead single from his sixth studio album Purple Rain. According to the DVD commentary of the film Purple Rain (1984), Prince was asked by director Albert Magnoli to write a song to match the theme of a particular segment of the film that involved Prince's character The Kid's intermingled parental difficulties with his father Francis L. and mother and a love affair with Apollonia. The next morning, Prince had composed two songs, one of which was "When Doves Cry". According to Prince's biographer Per Nilsen, the song was inspired by his relationship with Vanity 6 member Susan Moonsie.

sources.title: The Revolution (band)
sources.extract: The Revolution is an American funk rock band formed in Minneapolis, Minnesota, in 1979 by Prince, serving as his live band and later as his studio band. source.label: Wikipedia
source.title: Blood on the Tracks
source.extract: Blood on the Tracks is the fifteenth studio album by American singer-songwriter Bob Dylan, released on January 20, 1975, by Columbia Records. The album marked Dylan's return to Columbia after two albums with Asylum Records. Dylan began recording the album at an A & R studio in New York City in September 1974. In December, shortly before Columbia was due to release the album, Dylan abruptly re-recorded much of the material in Sound 80 studio in Minneapolis. The final album contains five tracks recorded in New York and five from Minneapolis. The songs have been linked to tensions in Dylan's personal life, including his estrangement from his then-wife Sara. One of their children, Jakob Dylan, described the songs as "my parents talking". Dylan has denied that the songs were autobiographical.

listeningNotes: On 'Tangled Up In Blue,' track the guitar’s open E tuning: the high strings ring out as drones while the bass notes walk, creating a sense of forward motion and simultaneous stasis that mirrors the lyric’s time-hopping.

Compare the New York and Minneapolis versions of 'Idiot Wind'—the album take features a Hammond organ swell at 2:10 that wasn’t on the original, and Dylan’s delivery is clipped and bitter, spitting the line 'You’re an idiot, babe' with a sneer absent from the earlier recording.

The harmonica solo on 'Simple Twist of Fate' enters at 1:52 with a dry, close-miked tone; it’s played in a rack, allowing Dylan to switch from guitar to harmonica without a pause, and the phrasing deliberately lags behind the beat.
Listen for the bass playing of Billy Peterson on the Minneapolis tracks—on 'Meet Me In the Morning,' his walking line is mixed unusually high, giving the blues shuffle a jazzy, conversational feel.

trackGuide.guide: A cubist narrative that jumps from a Minneapolis mattress to a topless joint to a parking lot in the rain, with the singer’s perspective shifting from first to third person. The guitar figure is a circular pattern in open E that never quite resolves, and the final verse recontextualizes every previous scene as a memory being recounted.

trackGuide.guide: A nine-minute frontier ballad with a cast of characters—a bank robber, an actor, a big-time operator—woven into a plot that turns on a hanging. sources.title: Idiot Wind
sources.extract: "Idiot Wind" is a song by Bob Dylan, which appeared on his 1975 album Blood on the Tracks. He began writing it in 1974, after his comeback tour with the Band. Dylan recorded the song in September 1974 and re-recorded it in December 1974 along with other songs on his album Blood on the Tracks. Between the recordings, he often reworked the lyrics. A live version of the song was released on Dylan's 1976 album Hard Rain, and all of the studio outtakes from the September sessions were released on the deluxe edition of The Bootleg Series Vol. 14: More Blood, More Tracks in 2018.

source.extract: The Miseducation of Lauryn Hill is the debut solo studio album by the American rapper and singer-songwriter Lauryn Hill. It was released on August 19, 1998, by Ruffhouse Records and Columbia Records. Recorded after Hill's band Fugees went on hiatus, the album is almost entirely written and produced by Hill. It is a concept album about educating oneself on love, with lyrical themes encompassing relationship complexities, interpersonal conflicts, motherhood, and faith. Predominantly a neo soul and R&B record, Miseducation also incorporates hip-hop, reggae, and soul, and features guest appearances from Carlos Santana, Mary J. Blige, and D'Angelo.

listeningNotes: The classroom skits between songs feature real students from Columbia High School in Maplewood, New Jersey; their unscripted reflections on love act as thematic bridges, and the teacher’s voice is Hill’s own slowed down.

On 'To Zion,' Carlos Santana’s guitar solo enters at 2:50 with a clean, singing tone that contrasts with the track’s hip-hop beat—his lines quote gospel phrasing, and the solo was recorded in a single take after Hill played him the song once.

The vocal duet on 'Nothing Even Matters' with D’Angelo was tracked live in the studio with both singers facing each other; listen for the way D’Angelo’s ad-libs at 3:10 weave around Hill’s lead, creating a counterpoint that feels improvised.

Hill’s production avoids samples entirely—the Fender Rhodes on 'Ex-Factor' plays a chord progression that echoes the Wu-Tang Clan’s 'Can It Be All So Simple' but is performed live, and the string arrangement was written by Hill and scored by a 12-piece section.

sources.label: Wikipedia
sources.title: Lauryn Hill
sources.extract: Lauryn Noelle Hill is an American singer, rapper, songwriter, record producer, and actress. She is considered one of the most influential musicians of her time, a pioneer of rap-singing, and a definitive figure in the neo soul movement. The Telegraph credited her with helping popularize hip-hop music. Hill was the only woman named on the lists of "Greatest MCs of All Time" (2006) by MTV and 10 Greatest Rappers by Billboard, and ranked the highest amongst women on the 2013 NME readers' poll of "Greatest Rappers Ever". She also appeared on Rolling Stone's 200 Greatest Singers, VH1's 100 Women in Music, and NPR's 50 Great Voices.

sources.title: The Miseducation of Lauryn Hill
sources.extract: The Miseducation of Lauryn Hill is the debut solo studio album by the American rapper and singer-songwriter Lauryn Hill. It was released on August 19, 1998, by Ruffhouse Records and Columbia Records. Recorded after Hill's band Fugees went on hiatus, the album is almost entirely written and produced by Hill. It is a concept album about educating oneself on love, with lyrical themes encompassing relationship complexities, interpersonal conflicts, motherhood, and faith. Predominantly a neo soul and R&B record, Miseducation also incorporates hip-hop, reggae, and soul, and features guest appearances from Carlos Santana, Mary J. Blige, and D'Angelo.

sources.title: Ex-Factor
sources.extract: "Ex-Factor" is a song by American recording artist Lauryn Hill for her debut solo studio album The Miseducation of Lauryn Hill (1998). Written and produced by Hill herself, it is a soul song. The song features a sample of "Can It Be All So Simple" by Wu-Tang Clan, hence its songwriters are also credited. It has been claimed to be about Hill's former Fugees groupmate Wyclef Jean. The song was released as the second single from The Miseducation of Lauryn Hill on December 14, 1998, by Ruffhouse Records and Columbia Records.

listeningNotes: On 'I'm Only Sleeping,' the reversed guitar solo enters at 0:10 and was created by Harrison working out the solo backwards, then reversing the tape so it plays forward with an eerie, liquid attack.

'Eleanor Rigby' features a double string quartet—four violins, two violas, two cellos—playing staccato chords with no Beatles instruments; listen for the close-miked cello that gives the low end its biting, percussive quality.

The final minute of 'Tomorrow Never Knows' swirls with five tape loops, including a sped-up seagull-like laugh and an orchestral chord from a Mellotron, all panned across the stereo field in real time during the mixdown.
McCartney double-tracked his vocal on 'Here, There and Everywhere' by singing the same part twice with identical phrasing, creating a halo effect that was later described as 'the perfect pop vocal.'

trackGuide.guide: Harrison's lead vocal on 'Taxman' drips with sarcasm over a descending bass line that quotes the Batman theme. The guitar solo, actually Paul McCartney playing a clipped, Indian-influenced line on his Epiphone Casino, was punched in at 1:10 and mimics the sound of a sitar.

sources.title: Taxman
sources.extract: "Taxman" is a song by the English rock band the Beatles from their 1966 album Revolver. Written by the group's lead guitarist, George Harrison, with some lyrical assistance from John Lennon, it protests against the higher level of progressive tax imposed in the United Kingdom by the Labour government of Harold Wilson, which saw the Beatles paying over 90 per cent of their earnings to the Treasury. The song was selected as the album's opening track and contributed to Harrison's emergence as a songwriter beside the dominant Lennon–McCartney partnership. It was the group's first topical song and the first political statement they had made in their music.

sources.title: Eleanor Rigby
sources.extract: "Eleanor Rigby" is a song by the English rock band the Beatles from their 1966 album Revolver. It was also issued on a double A-side single, paired with "Yellow Submarine". Credited to the Lennon–McCartney songwriting partnership, the song is one of only a few in which John Lennon and Paul McCartney later disputed primary authorship. Eyewitness testimony from several independent sources, including George Martin and Pete Shotton, supports McCartney's claim to authorship.

sources.title: I'm Only Sleeping
sources.extract: "I'm Only Sleeping" is a song by the English rock band the Beatles from their 1966 studio album Revolver. In the United States and Canada, it was one of the three tracks that Capitol Records cut from the album and instead included on Yesterday and Today, released two months before Revolver. Credited as a Lennon–McCartney song, it was written primarily by John Lennon. The track includes a backwards lead guitar part played by George Harrison, the first time such a technique was used on a pop recording.

sources.title: Love You To
sources.extract: "Love You To" is a song by the English rock band the Beatles from their 1966 album Revolver. The song was written and sung by George Harrison and features Indian instrumentation such as sitar and tabla. Following Harrison's introduction of the sitar on "Norwegian Wood " in 1965, it was the first Beatles song to fully reflect the influence of Indian classical music. The recording was made with minimal participation from Harrison's bandmates; instead, he created the track with tabla player Anil Bhagwat and other Indian musicians from the Asian Music Circle in London. The title references their first hit song; "Love Me Do".

sources.extract: "Here, There and Everywhere" is a song by the English rock band the Beatles from their 1966 album Revolver. A love ballad, it was written by Paul McCartney and credited to Lennon–McCartney. McCartney includes it among his personal favourites of the songs he has written. In 2000, Mojo ranked it 4th in the magazine's list of the greatest songs of all time.

sources.title: She Said She Said
sources.extract: "She Said She Said" is a song by the English rock band the Beatles from their 1966 album Revolver. Credited to Lennon–McCartney, it was written by John Lennon with assistance from George Harrison. Lennon described it as "an 'acidy' song" with lyrics inspired by actor Peter Fonda's comments during an LSD trip in August 1965 with members of the Beatles and the Byrds. "She Said She Said" was the last track recorded for Revolver. Due to an argument over the song's musical arrangement, Paul McCartney walked out of the studio during the song's recording, resulting in it being one of the few Beatles tracks to not feature McCartney in any capacity.

sources.label: Wikipedia
sources.title: For No One
sources.extract: "For No One" is a song by the English rock band the Beatles from their 1966 album Revolver. It was written by Paul McCartney, and credited to Lennon–McCartney. An early example of baroque pop drawing on both baroque music and nineteenth-century art song, it describes the end of a romantic relationship. Mostly performed by McCartney, the track is distinguished by its French horn line performed by Alan Civil, played first as a solo and then as counterpoint in the final verse. It was considered one of McCartney's most mature compositions to date on its release.

source.title: Thriller (album)
source.extract: Thriller is the sixth studio album by the American singer and songwriter Michael Jackson. It was released on November 29, 1982, through Epic Records. It was produced by Quincy Jones, who previously worked with Jackson on his album Off the Wall (1979). Recording took place from April to November 1982 at Westlake Recording Studios in Los Angeles, California, with a budget of $750,000. With the ongoing backlash against disco music, Jackson transitioned his sound, with Thriller featuring pop, post-disco, and R&B, while its themes include paranoia, romance, and social consciousness. Paul McCartney appears as the first credited featured artist on a Jackson album.

listeningNotes: The opening of 'Wanna Be Startin' Somethin'' layers a LinnDrum pattern, a synth bass line, and Jackson's percussive vocal gasps; the 'mama-se, mama-sa, ma-ma-coo-sa' chant at 4:40 was borrowed from Manu Dibango's 'Soul Makossa' and later settled out of court.

On 'Thriller,' the door creak at 0:22 is a real sound effect, and Vincent Price's rap was recorded in two takes—the second, more theatrical read was used. The bass line, played by Greg Phillinganes on a Minimoog, doubles the vocal melody.

Eddie Van Halen's guitar solo on 'Beat It' enters at 2:05 with a dive bomb; he played two takes, one of which was spliced together from different sections after he asked Jones to rearrange the tape to fit his improvisation.

'Billie Jean' features a bass line played by Louis Johnson on a Yamaha bass through a direct box, captured with a single SM57 mic placed on the amp's speaker cone. The finger snaps and the shaker were recorded in a dead booth, and Jackson's vocal was sung into a tube microphone with no compression.

trackGuide.guide: 'Wanna Be Startin' Somethin'' was written by Jackson and builds from a sparse funk groove into a frenzied climax. The horn arrangement by Jerry Hey punches in at 1:50, and the track's final two minutes are a call-and-response between Jackson's ad-libs and the backing choir.

sources.title: Michael Jackson
sources.extract: Michael Joseph Jackson was an American singer, songwriter, dancer, and philanthropist. Dubbed the "King of Pop", he is widely regarded as one of the most culturally significant figures of the 20th century. Over a four-decade career, his musical achievements broke American racial barriers and made him a dominant figure worldwide. Through his songs, concerts, and fashion, he proliferated visual performance for artists in popular music, popularizing street dance moves such as the moonwalk, the robot, and the anti-gravity lean. Jackson is often deemed the greatest entertainer of all time.

sources.title: Thriller (album)
sources.extract: Thriller is the sixth studio album by the American singer and songwriter Michael Jackson. It was released on November 29, 1982, through Epic Records. It was produced by Quincy Jones, who previously worked with Jackson on his album Off the Wall (1979). Recording took place from April to November 1982 at Westlake Recording Studios in Los Angeles, California, with a budget of $750,000. With the ongoing backlash against disco music, Jackson transitioned his sound, with Thriller featuring pop, post-disco, and R&B, while its themes include paranoia, romance, and social consciousness. Paul McCartney appears as the first credited featured artist on a Jackson album.

sources.title: Wanna Be Startin' Somethin'
sources.extract: "Wanna Be Startin'Somethin'" is a song by American singer Michael Jackson recorded for his sixth studio album Thriller (1982). It is the opening track of the album and was released as its fourth single on May 9, 1983, by Epic Records. It was written and co-produced by Jackson and produced by Quincy Jones. The lyrics pertain to strangers spreading rumors to start an argument for no good reason. "Wanna Be Startin'Somethin'" evokes the disco sound of Jackson's previous studio album, Off the Wall, released in 1979. The song is characterized by a complex rhythm arrangement and a distinctive horn arrangement.

sources.title: The Girl Is Mine
sources.extract: "The Girl Is Mine" is a song recorded by the American singer-songwriter Michael Jackson and the English singer-songwriter and musician Paul McCartney for Jackson's sixth solo album, Thriller. The track was written and co-produced by Jackson and produced by Quincy Jones. The song was recorded at Westlake Studios, Los Angeles, from April 14 to 16, 1982 and was released on October 18 of that same year as the album's first single. The year before, Jackson and McCartney had recorded "Say Say Say" and "The Man" for the latter's fifth solo album, Pipes of Peace (1983).

sources.title: Beat It
sources.extract: "Beat It" is a song by American singer Michael Jackson from his sixth studio album, Thriller (1982). It was written and composed by Jackson, produced by Quincy Jones, and co-produced by Jackson. Jones encouraged Jackson to include a rock song similar to "My Sharona" on the album. Jackson later said: "I wanted to write a song, the type of song that I would buy if I were to buy a rock song... And I wanted the children to really enjoy it — the school children as well as the college students." It includes a guitar solo by Eddie Van Halen.

sources.title: Billie Jean
sources.extract: "Billie Jean" is a song by the American singer Michael Jackson, released by Epic Records on January 2, 1983, as the second single from his sixth studio album, Thriller (1982). It was written by Jackson and produced by Jackson and Quincy Jones. "Billie Jean" blends post-disco, R&B, funk and dance-pop. The lyrics describe a young woman, Billie Jean, who claims that the narrator is the father of her newborn son, which he denies. Jackson said the lyrics were based on groupies' claims about his older brothers when he toured with them as the Jackson 5.

albumInfo.summary: I Never Loved a Man the Way I Love You is the ninth studio album by American singer Aretha Franklin, released on March 10, 1967, by Atlantic Records. It was Franklin's first release under her contract with the label, following her departure from Columbia Records after eight unsuccessful jazz standard albums, and marked a commercial breakthrough for her, becoming her first top 10 album in the United States, reaching number 2 on the Billboard 200. Two singles were released to promote the album: "Respect" and "I Never Loved a Man ".

listeningNotes: On 'Respect,' the horn section's punchy riff was arranged by Arif Mardin, and the 'sock it to me' call-and-response was a spontaneous studio invention by Carolyn Franklin; listen for the baritone sax growl at 1:10.

The title track opens with Spooner Oldham's electric piano and a slow, churchy organ swell; Aretha's vocal builds from a husky whisper to a full-throated belt over three minutes, with King Curtis's tenor sax solo entering at 2:00.

'Dr. Feelgood' is a slow blues with a spoken interlude at 1:35 where Aretha declares, 'I don't want nobody always sitting around me and my man,' delivered with conversational intimacy over Oldham's sustained organ chords.

'Do Right Woman, Do Right Man' features a country-soul piano intro by Oldham and a dual vocal by Aretha and her sisters, with the lyric 'a woman's only human' delivered as a quiet ultimatum over a swelling organ and brushed snare.

trackGuide.guide: Franklin's 'Respect' transforms Redding's original into a demand for dignity. The arrangement adds a bridge not in the original, and the background vocals spell 'R-E-S-P-E-C-T' with a syncopated rhythm. The track was cut in one take, with the horn section overdubbed later.

sources.title: I Never Loved a Man (The Way I Love You)
sources.extract: "I Never Loved a Man (The Way I Love You)" is a 1967 single released by American soul singer Aretha Franklin. Released on Atlantic Records as the first big hit of her career and the lead single from her ninth studio album of the same name, it became a defining song for Franklin, peaking at number one on the rhythm and blues charts and number nine on the pop charts. The B-side was "Do Right Woman, Do Right Man". Before this Franklin had placed only two Top 40 singles on the pop chart during her modest tenure with Columbia Records.

source.title: The Rolling Stones
source.extract: The Rolling Stones are an English rock band formed in London in 1962. Active for over six decades, they are one of the most popular, influential, and enduring bands of the rock era. In the early 1960s, the band pioneered the gritty, rhythmically driven sound that came to define hard rock. Their first stable line-up consisted of vocalist Mick Jagger, guitarist Keith Richards, multi-instrumentalist Brian Jones, bassist Bill Wyman, and drummer Charlie Watts, after pianist Ian Stewart was side-lined by their manager Andrew Loog Oldham. During their early years, Jones was the primary leader. Oldham encouraged them to write their own songs. The Jagger–Richards partnership soon became the band's primary songwriting and creative force.

albumInfo.summary: Exile on Main St. is the tenth studio album by the English rock band the Rolling Stones, released on 12 May 1972, by Rolling Stones Records. The 10th released in the UK and 12th in the US, it is viewed as a culmination of a string of the band's most critically successful albums, following Beggars Banquet (1968), Let It Bleed (1969) and Sticky Fingers (1971). Exile on Main St. is known for its wide stylistic range and the strong influence of Delta blues, gospel music, and country rock.

source.extract: Exile on Main St. is the tenth studio album by the English rock band the Rolling Stones, released on 12 May 1972, by Rolling Stones Records. The 10th released in the UK and 12th in the US, it is viewed as a culmination of a string of the band's most critically successful albums, following Beggars Banquet (1968), Let It Bleed (1969) and Sticky Fingers (1971). Exile on Main St. is known for its wide stylistic range and the strong influence of Delta blues, gospel music, and country rock. The album was originally met with mixed reviews before receiving strong reassessments by the end of the 1970s. It has since been recognized as a pivotal rock album, viewed by many critics as the Rolling Stones' best work and as one of the greatest albums of all time.

sources.title: The Rolling Stones
sources.extract: The Rolling Stones are an English rock band formed in London in 1962. Active for over six decades, they are one of the most popular, influential, and enduring bands of the rock era. In the early 1960s, the band pioneered the gritty, rhythmically driven sound that came to define hard rock. Their first stable line-up consisted of vocalist Mick Jagger, guitarist Keith Richards, multi-instrumentalist Brian Jones, bassist Bill Wyman, and drummer Charlie Watts, after pianist Ian Stewart was side-lined by their manager Andrew Loog Oldham. During their early years, Jones was the primary leader. Oldham encouraged them to write their own songs. The Jagger–Richards partnership soon became the band's primary songwriting and creative force.

sources.title: Exile on Main St.
sources.extract: Exile on Main St. is the tenth studio album by the English rock band the Rolling Stones, released on 12 May 1972, by Rolling Stones Records. The 10th released in the UK and 12th in the US, it is viewed as a culmination of a string of the band's most critically successful albums, following Beggars Banquet (1968), Let It Bleed (1969) and Sticky Fingers (1971). Exile on Main St. is known for its wide stylistic range and the strong influence of Delta blues, gospel music, and country rock. The album was originally met with mixed reviews before receiving strong reassessments by the end of the 1970s. It has since been recognized as a pivotal rock album, viewed by many critics as the Rolling Stones' best work and as one of the greatest albums of all time.

source.title: Public Enemy
source.extract: Public Enemy is an American hip-hop group formed in Roosevelt, New York, in 1985 by Chuck D and Flavor Flav. The group rose to prominence for their political messages including subjects such as American racism and the American media. Their debut album, Yo! Bum Rush the Show, was released in 1987 to critical acclaim, and their second album, It Takes a Nation of Millions to Hold Us Back (1988), was the first hip-hop album to top The Village Voice's Pazz & Jop critics' poll. Their next three albums, Fear of a Black Planet (1990), Apocalypse 91... The Enemy Strikes Black (1991), and Muse Sick-n-Hour Mess Age (1994), were also well received. The group has since released eleven more studio albums, including the soundtrack to the 1998 sports-drama film He Got Game and a collaborative album with Paris, Rebirth of a Nation (2006). Their most recent album, Black Sky Over the Projects: Apartment 2025, was released in 2025.

source.extract: The Clash were an English rock band formed in London in 1976. Billed as "The Only Band That Matters", they are considered one of the most influential acts in the original wave of British punk rock, with their music fusing elements of reggae, dub, funk, ska and rockabilly. listeningNotes: The opening guitar riff of 'London Calling' spells out the Morse code for S.O.S. (dot-dot-dot dash-dash-dash dot-dot-dot), played by Mick Jones on a Les Paul Junior through a cranked amplifier.
Paul Simonon's lead vocal debut on 'The Guns of Brixton' rides a deep reggae bass line he wrote; the toasting-style backing vocals by Joe Strummer and Jones mimic Jamaican deejay techniques.
'Spanish Bombs' double-tracks Strummer's vocals in English and Spanish, blending a flamenco-tinged guitar line with a punk chorus; the lyrics juxtapose the Spanish Civil War with modern tourism.

'Train In Vain' was originally not listed on the sleeve; listen for the harmonica solo at 1:50, played by Jones, and the train-rhythm guitar chug that gives the song its title despite never being mentioned in the lyrics.

sources.title: The Clash
sources.extract: The Clash were an English rock band formed in London in 1976. Billed as "The Only Band That Matters", they are considered one of the most influential acts in the original wave of British punk rock, with their music fusing elements of reggae, dub, funk, ska and rockabilly. The band also contributed to the post-punk and new wave movements that followed. For most of their recording career, the Clash consisted of lead vocalist and rhythm guitarist Joe Strummer, lead guitarist and vocalist Mick Jones, bassist Paul Simonon and drummer Nicky "Topper" Headon.

Billed as "The Only Band That Matters", they are considered one of the most influential acts in the original wave of British punk rock, with their music fusing elements of reggae, dub, funk, ska and rockabilly. The band also contributed to the post-punk and new wave movements that followed.

sources.title: Brand New Cadillac
sources.extract: "Brand New Cadillac" is a 1959 song by Vince Taylor, and was originally released as a B-side. Featured musicians on the released recording were: Joe Moretti (guitars), Lou Brian (piano), Brian Locking (bass) and Brian Bennett (drums). While not successful in the UK, it got a huge surge in popularity in continental Europe, especially the Nordic countries, with acts such as the Renegades and Hep Stars bringing it to number one in Finland and Sweden, respectively. Another Swedish act, the Shamrocks, brought the song to number one in France.

sources.title: Lost in the Supermarket
sources.extract: "Lost in the Supermarket" is a song by the English punk rock band the Clash. Written by Joe Strummer and Mick Jones and produced by Guy Stevens, it is credited to the Strummer/Jones songwriting partnership. It was released on their third studio album, London Calling, and appears as the eighth song on the track listing. Although it features Jones on lead vocals, the song was written by Strummer. The supermarket in question was the International, located at 471–473 Kings Road, beneath the World's End Estate. Strummer lived at 31 Whistler Walk at the time with his girlfriend Gaby Salter, her two younger brothers and her mother. The song appears in the Apple TV+ show Loot.

It was released on their third studio album, London Calling, and appears as the eighth song on the track listing.

sources.title: Clampdown
sources.extract: "Clampdown" is a song by the English rock band the Clash from their 1979 album London Calling. The song began as an instrumental track called "Working and Waiting". It is sometimes called "Working for the Clampdown", which is the main lyric of the song and also the title provided on the album's lyric sheet. Its lyrics concern those who have forsaken the idealism of youth and urges young people to fight the status quo. The word "clampdown" is a neat cover-all term the writers adopted to define the oppressive Establishment, notably its more reactionary voices who were to be heard throughout the 1970s calling alarmingly for "clampdowns" by government and law enforcement on strikers, agitators, benefits claimants, football hooligans, punks and other perceived threats to the social, economic and moral wellbeing of the UK.

sources.title: Train in Vain
sources.extract: "Train in Vain" (or "Train in Vain (Stand by Me)") is a song by the English punk rock band the Clash. It was released as the third and final single from their third studio album, London Calling (1979). The song was not originally listed on the album's track listing, appearing as a hidden track at the end of the album. This was because the track was added to the record at the last minute, when the sleeve was already in production. Some editions include the song in the track listing. "Train in Vain" was the first single by the Clash to reach the Top 40 of the Billboard Hot 100 chart in the United States and in 2010, the song was ranked number 298 on Rolling Stone magazine's list of The 500 Greatest Songs of All Time.

listeningNotes: 'Dark Fantasy' opens with a choral arrangement by Nicki Minaj, who narrates a twisted fairy tale in a British accent; Teyana Taylor's vocals enter at 0:30, and the beat drops at 1:00 with a sample of Mike Oldfield's 'In High Places.'

The 'Power' beat is built around a sample of King Crimson's '21st Century Schizoid Man' pitched up, with handclaps and a distorted 808; the breakdown at 2:10 strips to a piano and a chant, then rebuilds with a choir.

Nicki Minaj's verse on 'Monster' at 3:35 is a show-stealing 32-bar performance where she switches between multiple personas—a demonic growl, a valley girl, and a Roman empress—recorded in one take after she heard Jay-Z's verse.

The last three minutes of 'Runaway' feature West singing through a vocoder with heavy distortion, creating a wordless, wounded cry over a simple piano loop and a cello line; the guitar feedback was added by Mike Dean.

source.extract: Bob Dylan is an American singer-songwriter. Described as one of the greatest songwriters of all time, Dylan has been a major figure in popular culture over his 69-year career. With an estimated 125 million records sold worldwide, he is one of the best-selling musicians. Dylan added increasingly sophisticated lyrical techniques to the folk music of the early 1960s, infusing it "with the intellectualism of classic literature and poetry". His lyrics incorporated political, social, and philosophical influences, defying pop music conventions and appealing to the burgeoning counterculture.

albumInfo.summary: Highway 61 Revisited is the sixth studio album by the American singer-songwriter Bob Dylan, released on August 30, 1965, by Columbia Records. Dylan continued the musical approach of his previous album Bringing It All Back Home (1965), using rock musicians as his backing band on every track of the album in a further departure from his primarily acoustic folk sound, except for the closing track, the 11-minute ballad "Desolation Row". Critics have focused on the innovative way Dylan combined driving, blues-based music with the subtlety of poetry to create songs that captured the political and cultural climate of contemporary America.

listeningNotes: Al Kooper's improvised organ riff on 'Like a Rolling Stone'—he wasn't an organist, just sat at the instrument during the session.
The snare drum crack that opens 'Like a Rolling Stone' was a happy accident: drummer Bobby Gregg hit it to signal the take, and they kept it.
On 'Ballad of a Thin Man,' the descending piano chords and ghostly organ create an ominous atmosphere; Dylan's sneering delivery paints a character study of confusion.
'Desolation Row' is an 11-minute acoustic track with only Dylan's guitar, harmonica, and Charlie McCoy's subtle bass harmonica, contrasting the electric band elsewhere.

trackGuide.guide: The opening snare shot and Kooper's organ swell set the stage for a torrent of vitriol aimed at a fallen socialite. Bloomfield's lead guitar fills are sharp and bluesy, while the chorus's 'How does it feel?' became a generational rallying cry.

trackGuide.guide: A rapid-fire blues rocker with surreal imagery (Galileo, Belle Starr, John the Baptist). Bloomfield's stinging guitar and Kooper's barrelhouse piano drive the track, while Dylan's vocal phrasing is relentlessly syncopated.

sources.label: Wikipedia
sources.title: Bob Dylan
sources.extract: Bob Dylan is an American singer-songwriter. Described as one of the greatest songwriters of all time, Dylan has been a major figure in popular culture over his 69-year career. With an estimated 125 million records sold worldwide, he is one of the best-selling musicians. Dylan added increasingly sophisticated lyrical techniques to the folk music of the early 1960s, infusing it "with the intellectualism of classic literature and poetry". His lyrics incorporated political, social, and philosophical influences, defying pop music conventions and appealing to the burgeoning counterculture.

sources.label: Wikipedia
sources.title: Highway 61 Revisited
sources.extract: Highway 61 Revisited is the sixth studio album by the American singer-songwriter Bob Dylan, released on August 30, 1965, by Columbia Records. Dylan continued the musical approach of his previous album Bringing It All Back Home (1965), using rock musicians as his backing band on every track of the album in a further departure from his primarily acoustic folk sound, except for the closing track, the 11-minute ballad "Desolation Row". Critics have focused on the innovative way Dylan combined driving, blues-based music with the subtlety of poetry to create songs that captured the political and cultural climate of contemporary America. Author Michael Gray argued that, in an important sense, the 1960s "started" with this album.

sources.title: Like a Rolling Stone
sources.extract: "Like a Rolling Stone" is a song by American singer-songwriter Bob Dylan that was released on July 20, 1965 by Columbia Records. Its confrontational lyrics originated in an extended piece of verse Dylan wrote in June 1965, when he returned exhausted from a grueling tour of England. Dylan distilled this draft into four verses and a chorus. He recorded "Like a Rolling Stone" a few weeks later as the opening track of his sixth studio album, Highway 61 Revisited. During a difficult two-day preproduction, Dylan struggled to find the essence of the song, which was demoed without success in 34 time. A breakthrough happened when he recorded it in a rock format and rookie session musician Al Kooper improvised a Hammond organ riff.

sources.label: Wikipedia
sources.title: Just Like Tom Thumb's Blues
sources.extract: "Just Like Tom Thumb's Blues" is a song written and performed by Bob Dylan. It was originally recorded on August 2, 1965, and released on the album Highway 61 Revisited. The song was later released on the compilation album Bob Dylan's Greatest Hits Vol. II and as two separate live versions recorded at concerts in 1966: the first of which appeared on the B-side of Dylan's "I Want You" single, with the second being released on The Bootleg Series Vol. 4: Bob Dylan Live 1966, The "Royal Albert Hall" Concert. The song has been covered by many artists, including Gordon Lightfoot, Cat Power, Nina Simone, Barry McGuire, Judy Collins, Frankie Miller, Linda Ronstadt, the Grateful Dead, Neil Young, The Black Crowes, Townes Van Zandt, Bryan Ferry, and The Handsome Family. Lightfoot's version was recorded only weeks after Dylan's original had been released and reached #3 on the Canadian RPM singles chart.

sources.title: Desolation Row
sources.extract: "Desolation Row" is a song by the American singer-songwriter Bob Dylan. It was recorded on August 4, 1965, and released as the closing track of Dylan's sixth studio album, Highway 61 Revisited. The song has been noted for its length (11:21) and surreal lyrics in which Dylan weaves characters into a series of vignettes that suggest entropy and urban chaos.

listeningNotes: The production uses a warm, analog sound with heavy bass, Fender Rhodes, and layered horns, recorded largely live in the studio.
Kendrick's vocal delivery constantly shifts: from a desperate howl on 'u' to a calm, childlike tone on 'For Free?' to a boastful flow on 'King Kunta.'
A recurring poem begins on 'Wesley's Theory' and builds across tracks, finally revealed in full on 'Mortal Man' as a letter to Tupac.
Seamless transitions between songs, with interludes and sound collages that mimic a radio dial or internal monologue, create a continuous narrative flow.

trackGuide.guide: Opens with a sample of Boris Gardiner's 'Every Nigger is a Star' and a funky bassline by Thundercat. Kendrick raps about the traps of fame and money, with George Clinton's cosmic ad-libs. The chorus's 'Wesley's Theory' refers to Wesley Snipes' tax evasion, a cautionary tale.

sources.extract: "King Kunta" is a song by American hip-hop recording artist Kendrick Lamar, from his third album, To Pimp a Butterfly (2015). It was released as the album's third single on March 24, 2015. Lamar co-wrote the song with Thundercat, while Terrace Martin, Michael Kuhle, and Sounwave served as producers. sources.title: The Blacker the Berry (song)
sources.extract: "The Blacker the Berry" is a song by American rapper Kendrick Lamar. It was included as the thirteenth track from his third studio album To Pimp a Butterfly (2015). "The Blacker the Berry" was released as the second single from the album on February 9, 2015. The track shares its title with American author Wallace Thurman's novel The Blacker the Berry (1929) and a lyric from Tupac Shakur's "Keep Ya Head Up" (1993). "The Blacker the Berry" was produced by Boi-1da, Terrace Martin, and KOZ, as well as containing a chorus that features uncredited vocals from Jamaican artist Assassin and additional vocals provided by singer Lalah Hathaway.

listeningNotes: 'Everything In Its Right Place' uses a 10/4 time signature and a chopped, stuttering vocal loop; the Fender Rhodes riff is hypnotic and never fully resolves.
On 'The National Anthem,' a chaotic free-jazz horn section enters at 2:45, recorded by musicians instructed to sound like a traffic jam.
'Idioteque' is built on a sample from Paul Lansky's computer music piece 'Mild und Leise' and a drum machine pattern; Yorke's lyrics were drawn from a hat.
'Motion Picture Soundtrack' features angelic harmonium and harp, with Yorke's voice layered into a choir; after a long silence, a hidden ambient track (Untitled) provides a brief, gentle coda.

trackGuide.guide: Opens with a warm, repetitive Rhodes keyboard riff, then Yorke's vocals enter, digitally manipulated into a staccato pattern. The song's structure is circular, never fully resolving, mirroring the dislocation of the digital age.

sources.title: Kid A
sources.extract: Kid A is the fourth studio album by the English rock band Radiohead, released on 2 October 2000 by Parlophone. It was recorded with their producer, Nigel Godrich, in Paris, Copenhagen, Gloucestershire and Oxfordshire. Departing from their earlier sound, Radiohead incorporated influences from electronic music, krautrock, jazz and 20th-century classical music, with a wider range of instruments and effects. The singer, Thom Yorke, wrote abstract lyrics, cutting up phrases and assembling them at random.

listeningNotes: 'Thunder Road' opens with a harmonica and piano, building to a full-band crescendo; listen for Roy Bittan's piano runs and the way Springsteen's voice cracks with desperation.
'Born to Run' required 72 channels of overdubs to achieve its dense Wall of Sound, featuring multiple guitar tracks and Clarence Clemons' iconic sax solo.
'Backstreets' begins with a long piano intro, and Springsteen's raw vocal tells a story of friendship and betrayal, with organ swells and guitar feedback adding dramatic tension.
'Jungleland' is a 9-minute epic with a violin solo by Suki Lahav and a legendary sax break from Clemons that lasts over two minutes.

It was Springsteen's first worldwide single release, although it achieved little initial success outside of the United States. The single was also Springsteen's first Top 40 hit on the Billboard Hot 100, peaking at No. 23.

listeningNotes: The album is structured as a concept: 'Intro' depicts his birth, and 'Suicidal Thoughts' ends with a gunshot and a flatline, completing the life-to-death arc.
'Gimme the Loot' features Biggie switching between two voices—a high-pitched stick-up kid and a lower growl—all performed by him.
'Juicy' samples Mtume's 'Juicy Fruit' and transforms it into a rags-to-riches anthem; notice the contrast between the grim verses and the celebratory chorus.
'The What' is a collaboration with Method Man, the only guest rapper, and their back-and-forth chemistry is electric over a menacing beat.

source.title: The Velvet Underground & Nico
source.extract: The Velvet Underground & Nico is the debut studio album by the Velvet Underground and Nico, released by Verve Records in March 1967. Recorded in 1966 while the group were associated with Andy Warhol's Exploding Plastic Inevitable, it was co-produced by Warhol and Tom Wilson. source.title: Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band
source.extract: Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band is the eighth studio album by the English rock band the Beatles. Released on 26 May 1967, Sgt. Pepper is regarded by musicologists as an early concept album that advanced the roles of sound composition, extended form, psychedelic imagery, record sleeves, and the producer in popular music. The album had an immediate cross-generational impact and was associated with numerous touchstones of the era's youth culture, such as fashion, drugs, mysticism, and a sense of optimism and empowerment. Critics lauded the album for its innovations in songwriting, production and graphic design, for bridging a cultural divide between popular music and high art, and for reflecting the interests of contemporary youth and the counterculture.

listeningNotes: Listen for the audience murmur and orchestra tuning that crossfade from the title track into 'With a Little Help from My Friends,' creating the illusion of a continuous live show.

In 'Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds,' John Lennon's vocal was recorded at a slower speed then sped up, giving it a reedy, otherworldly timbre; the droning tambura and Lowrey organ part reinforce the hallucinatory imagery.
'She's Leaving Home' features no Beatles instrumentation—only a ten-piece string section arranged by Mike Leander, with the harp's ascending glissando at 1:42 mirroring the girl's escape.

The final piano chord of 'A Day in the Life' was played simultaneously on three pianos by Lennon, McCartney, Ringo Starr, and Mal Evans, with the fader raised for 40 seconds to capture the full decay of the note.

trackGuide.guide: 'A Day in the Life' stitches together two unfinished Lennon and McCartney songs, bridged by a 40-piece orchestra instructed to ascend from their lowest note to their highest over 24 bars. The final E-major piano chord, which lasts over 40 seconds, was recorded with the studio's compressors maxed out, and the vinyl pressing includes a 15-kilohertz tone and a loop of gibberish in the run-out groove.

sources.title: Within You Without You
sources.extract: "Within You Without You" is a song by the English rock band The Beatles from their 1967 album Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band. Written by lead guitarist George Harrison, it was his second composition in the Indian classical style, after "Love You To", and inspired by his stay in India in late 1966 with his mentor and sitar teacher Ravi Shankar. Recorded in London without the other Beatles, it features Indian instrumentation such as sitar, tambura, dilruba and tabla, and was performed by Harrison and members of the Asian Music Circle. The recording marked a significant departure from the Beatles' previous work; musically, it evokes the Indian devotional tradition, while the overtly spiritual quality of the lyrics reflects Harrison's absorption in Hindu philosophy and the teachings of the Vedas.

listeningNotes: The opening piano riff of 'I Feel the Earth Move' is a percussive, syncopated figure that King pounds out with gospel fervor; listen for the way her vocal cracks slightly on the word 'mellow' at 0:48.
In 'It's Too Late,' the iconic saxophone solo by Curtis Amy enters at 1:56, its breathy tone and melodic contour mirroring the resigned sadness of the lyric.

On 'Will You Love Me Tomorrow?,' Joni Mitchell joins James Taylor on backing vocals, their harmonies floating behind King's lead; the arrangement shifts from a sparse piano-and-strings verse to a fuller chorus with brushed drums.

'(You Make Me Feel Like) A Natural Woman' was co-written with Gerry Goffin and Jerry Wexler, and King's piano accompaniment builds from gospel-tinged chords to a triumphant ascending run leading into the final chorus at 2:45.

sources.label: Wikipedia
sources.title: Writer (album)
sources.extract: Writer is the debut studio album by American singer-songwriter Carole King, released in May 1970. King already had a successful career as a songwriter, and been a part of The City, a short-lived group she formed after moving to Los Angeles in 1968. Tracks on the album include "Up on the Roof" which was a number 4 hit for the Drifters in 1962, and "Child of Mine", which has been recorded by Billy Joe Royal, among others. The album did not receive much attention upon its release, though it entered the chart following the success of King's next album, Tapestry, in 1971. It was produced by John Fischbach, the co-founder of Crystal Sound studio, in Hollywood, California, where the album was recorded.

sources.title: I Feel the Earth Move
sources.extract: "I Feel the Earth Move" is a song written and performed by American singer-songwriter Carole King, for her second studio album Tapestry (1971). Additionally, the song is one half of the double A-sided single, the flip side of which was "It's Too Late". Together, both "I Feel the Earth Move" and "It's Too Late" became among the biggest mainstream pop hits of 1971.

sources.title: You've Got a Friend
sources.extract: "You've Got a Friend" is a 1971 song and single by American singer-songwriter Carole King. It was first recorded by King and included on her second studio album, Tapestry (1971). Another well-known version by James Taylor appears on his album Mud Slide Slim and the Blue Horizon (1971). His version, which features backing vocals by Joni Mitchell, was released as a single in 1971, reaching number one on the Billboard Hot 100 and number four on the UK Singles Chart. The two versions were recorded simultaneously in 1971 with some shared musicians.

sources.title: Where You Lead
sources.extract: "Where You Lead" is a song written in 1970 by Carole King with lyricist Toni Stern, introduced on King's iconic 1971 album Tapestry. A Top 40 hit for Barbra Streisand in both a studio version from her 1971 album Barbra Joan Streisand and a live version featured on her 1972 album Live Concert at the Forum—the latter in a medley titled "Sweet Inspiration/Where You Lead"—the song has also served as the main theme song for the 2000-2007 The WB dramedy series Gilmore Girls in a lyrically revised version recorded by King and Louise Goffin and was featured on the 2002 soundtrack album Our Little Corner of the World: Music from Gilmore Girls.

sources.title: Will You Love Me Tomorrow
sources.extract: "Will You Love Me Tomorrow" is a song written by Gerry Goffin and Carole King. It was first recorded in 1960 by the Shirelles for their album Tonight's the Night; released as a single that November, it became the first song by a girl group to top the Billboard Hot 100 chart. It has since been recorded by many other artists, including King on her 1971 album Tapestry.

sources.title: (You Make Me Feel Like) A Natural Woman
sources.extract: "(You Make Me Feel Like) A Natural Woman" is a 1967 song recorded by American soul singer Aretha Franklin and released as a single by Atlantic from her album Lady Soul. The lyrics were written by Gerry Goffin from an idea by Atlantic producer Jerry Wexler, with music composed by Carole King. Created specifically for Franklin, the single reached number 8 on the Billboard Hot 100 and became one of her signature recordings. It entered the UK Singles Chart at number 79 in 2018, one week after Franklin's death, marking its first appearance there more than 50 years after its original release. Franklin later included a live version on her 1968 album Aretha in Paris.
